title: Dance & Music
desc: Traditional Nauruan dance tells stories of the ocean, the harvest, and community life. Rhythmic movements passed down through generations.
details: Traditional Nauruan dance is characterized by rhythmic hip movements, synchronized hand gestures, and vibrant costumes made from pandanus leaves and coconut fibers. Dances tell stories of ocean voyages, harvest celebrations, and ancestral legends. The most well-known traditional performance is the 'ekorere' — a seated dance using hand and upper body movements. Music traditionally features percussion instruments including the body of the dance drum and bamboo stamping tubes. Today, modern Nauruan music blends these traditional rhythms with Pacific reggae and contemporary pop. Church choirs are also a significant part of Nauruan musical culture, with four-part harmonies being especially popular.

title: Island Flavors
desc: Coconut, fresh fish, breadfruit, and pandanus — Nauruan cuisine is pure Pacific. Try coconut-crusted reef fish.
details: Nauruan cuisine is built around what the ocean and land provide. Fresh reef fish (tuna, mahi-mahi, snapper) is the protein staple, often prepared grilled, raw in coconut lime marinade, or fried. Coconut appears in nearly every meal — as coconut cream in curries, grated over fish, or as refreshing coconut water. Breadfruit, pandanus fruit, and当地 bananas grow on the island and are prepared in numerous ways: roasted, boiled, fried into chips, or fermented for preservation. A traditional specialty is coconut fish — fresh raw fish marinated in fresh lime juice and coconut cream, served with breadfruit chips. Another is 'ika mata' — the Nauruan take on the classic Pacific raw fish salad. Meals are often communal, with extended family sharing dishes served on banana or pandanus leaves.

title: Celebrations
desc: Angam Day (Oct 26) celebrates population resilience. Constitution Day (May 17) is a week-long community festival.
details: Angam Day (October 26) is Nauru's most significant cultural celebration, commemorating the return of the Nauruan population to 1,500 — the minimum considered necessary for survival after the devastating flu epidemics of 1920 and the WWII forced relocation. The day features traditional dance competitions between districts, choral singing contests, sports tournaments, and community feasts. Constitution Day (May 17) celebrates the 1968 constitution with a week-long festival including parades, live music concerts, traditional craft exhibitions, and the Miss Nauru pageant. Independence Day (January 31) marks Nauru's 1968 independence and includes government ceremonies, flag-raising at sunrise, and community sports events. Other notable celebrations include Christmas (with unique Nauruan carols), Easter, and National Youth Day.

title: Handicrafts & Art
desc: Traditional Nauruan weaving, carving, and crafting using pandanus and coconut fibers — a living heritage.
details: Nauruan women are renowned for their intricate weaving skills, creating baskets, mats, hats, and fans from pandanus leaves. The leaves are harvested, dried in the sun, split into strips, and dyed using natural pigments from plants and soils. Patterns are geometric and often carry symbolic meaning representing ocean waves, fish scales, or turtle shells. Men traditionally carve wood and coconut shells into tools, bowls, and decorative items. The frigate bird — Nauru's national symbol — appears frequently in Nauruan art. While many traditional crafts declined during the phosphate boom years, there has been a cultural renaissance in recent decades, with workshops teaching younger generations these ancestral skills. The Nauru Museum in Yaren showcases the finest examples of traditional craftsmanship.

title: Community Life
desc: Nauruan society is built on extended family bonds, the concept of 'engam' (mutual support), and close-knit community structures.
details: Nauruan social structure centers around the extended family (known as 'te' rather than the English term) and the 12 traditional tribes that once governed social organization. While the tribal system no longer has formal governance roles, it remains an important part of Nauruan identity. The concept of 'engam' — mutual support and sharing within the community — is deeply embedded in Nauruan values. Sunday church attendance is near-universal, and the island virtually shuts down for worship. Community events, whether church gatherings, sports tournaments (especially Australian rules football and weightlifting), or district celebrations, are central to Nauruan social life. Elders are respected figures, and their wisdom is sought in family and community decisions.
